platforms.title: 5 Signs a Swollen Gland in Your Neck Needs a GP
platforms.meta_description: Found a lump in your neck after a cold? NHS advice says most swollen glands go down in 1 to 2 weeks. Here are the 5 signs that mean you should see a GP.
platforms.body_html:
You are drying your face after a shower, your fingers run along your jaw, and there it is: a small, slightly sore bump under the skin. If you have just had a cold or a sore throat, the timing is probably not a coincidence. According to the NHS, swollen glands are usually a sign the body is fighting an infection, and glands swollen by an infection usually get better by themselves within 1 to 2 weeks. The useful question is not "is this cancer?" but "does this lump match the pattern of a normal infection, or not?"

Why the glands in your neck swell

The "glands" people feel in their neck are lymph glands, also called lymph nodes. They sit along both sides of the neck, under the chin, in the armpits and around the groin. The NHS explains that glands swell near an infection to help your body fight it. A throat, ear or tooth infection drains into the nodes in your neck, so that is where the swelling shows up.

Infection-related swelling has a recognisable feel. The NHS describes swollen glands as tender, painful lumps, and you may also have a sore throat, a cough or a high temperature at the same time. Sometimes a gland on just one side of the body swells. The usual triggers are ordinary: colds, tonsillitis, and ear or throat infections. Viral infections such as glandular fever are a less common cause. The NHS states that swollen glands are only rarely caused by something more serious, such as cancer of the blood (leukaemia) or of the lymph system (lymphoma).

That last point matters because it explains why doctors look for a pattern rather than reacting to every lump. A gland that appears with a cold, feels tender and shrinks as you recover fits the infection pattern. A gland that keeps growing, feels hard, or turns up with no illness at all does not, and that is when it is worth a professional look.

5 signs it is time to book a GP appointment

The NHS lists clear reasons to see a GP if you have swollen glands. Each one is a way the lump breaks the normal infection pattern:

  • They are getting bigger, or have not gone down within 1 week. Infection-driven swelling should be heading in the right direction, not growing.
  • They feel hard or do not move when you press them. The NHS describes infection-swollen glands as tender, painful lumps instead.
  • You are having night sweats or a very high temperature, meaning you feel hot, cold or shivery.
  • You have no other signs of illness or infection. A lump that turns up out of nowhere has no obvious cause to explain it.
  • The swelling is just above or below your collarbone, the bone that runs from your breastbone to each shoulder.

Until then, the NHS self-care advice is simple: rest, drink plenty of fluids to avoid dehydration, and take painkillers like paracetamol or ibuprofen if the glands are sore. Do not give aspirin to children under 16. It also helps to note the date you first noticed the lump and roughly how big it is, so you can tell whether it is shrinking and give your GP a clear history.

If you do one thing today

Put a reminder in your phone for one week from today that simply says "neck lump: smaller?". When it pops up, feel the area again. If it has gone down and your cold has cleared, that fits the usual course. If it is the same size or bigger, or you have spotted any of the five signs above, book a GP appointment rather than waiting another few weeks.

It helps to know what the GP is weighing up. NICE guideline NG12 on suspected cancer, which GPs in England follow, tells them to consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for Hodgkin lymphoma in adults with unexplained lymphadenopathy (swollen lymph nodes with no clear cause). It asks them to take into account symptoms such as fever, night sweats, shortness of breath, itching, weight loss or lymph node pain after drinking alcohol. For people aged 45 and over, NG12 lists an unexplained lump in the neck as a reason to consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for laryngeal cancer. For children and young people with unexplained swollen nodes, it recommends considering a very urgent referral, meaning an appointment within 48 hours. The NHS itself stresses that serious causes of swollen glands are rare; the referral route exists so that a rare serious cause is not missed.

One situation should not wait at all. The NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if you have swollen glands and you are finding it very difficult to swallow or have difficulty breathing. A GP will recommend treatment depending on the cause, which might include antibiotics, although antibiotics do not work on viral infections.

This article is general information and does not replace advice from your GP. Do not self-diagnose; if you are worried about a lump, see a GP.

Sources: NHS, "Swollen glands" (page last reviewed 29 September 2023); NICE guideline NG12, "Suspected cancer: recognition and referral" (last updated 15 April 2026).
